Osmotic pressure follows the van't Hoff equation, which has the same form as the gas law:
π = iCRT
where C is the molar concentration of the solute and T the absolute temperature.
(1) Raising T raises π directly, since π ∝ T ✓
(2) Lowering T lowers it — the opposite.
(3) Increasing the volume of the vessel spreads the same solute through more solvent, so C falls
and π falls with it.
(4) Diluting likewise reduces C and therefore π.
So only one of the four pushes π up.
∴ by increasing the temperature of the solution.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|8||0|0.s:
Work out the electrons needed, then convert to faradays.
In Cr₂O₇²⁻, each oxygen is −2, so 2x + 7(−2) = −2, giving x = +6. Each chromium is Cr(VI).
The product is Cr³⁺, so each chromium goes +6 ⇒ +3, a gain of 3 electrons.
One dichromate ion contains two chromiums:
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ ⇒ 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O
So 1 mol of Cr₂O₇²⁻ needs 6 mol of electrons.
One faraday is one mole of electrons, so the charge required is 6 F.
The common slip is to answer 3 F by forgetting there are two chromium atoms in the ion.
∴ 6 F.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|9||0|0:
The rate law is given as r = k[A]², so the reaction is second order in A.
Let the original rate be r₁ = k[A]².
Double the concentration: the new rate is r₂ = k(2[A])² = k·4[A]² = 4·k[A]²
r₂/r₁ = 4
The exponent is what matters, not the stoichiometric coefficient m — doubling a reactant
multiplies the rate by 2^(order).
So first order would double it, second order quadruples it, third order would give eight times.
∴ the rate is quadrupled.
kcet|Chemistry|2016|10||0|0:
A Schottky defect is a vacancy defect, and the crystal must stay electrically neutral.
So cations and anions have to leave in numbers that balance the charge — for a 1:1 salt like
NaCl that means equal numbers of each.
(1) Unequal numbers would leave the crystal charged, which cannot happen.
(3) An ion leaving its site for an interstitial site is the *Frenkel* defect, not Schottky.
(4) No ion missing is a perfect crystal, not a defect at all.
Because ions are genuinely removed, the mass of the unit cell falls while its volume does not,
so a Schottky defect lowers the density — the main way it is told apart from Frenkel, which
leaves density unchanged.
It is shown by ionic solids with similar cation and anion sizes and high coordination number:
NaCl, KCl, CsCl, AgBr.
∴ equal numbers of cations and anions are missing from the lattice.
kcet|Chemistry|2016|11||0|0:
For a reaction aA ⇒ bB the single rate of reaction is each species' rate divided by its coefficient:
rate = −(1/a)·d[A]/dt = (1/b)·d[B]/dt
Here the reaction is 3A ⇒ 2B, so a = 3 and b = 2:
−(1/3)·d[A]/dt = (1/2)·d[B]/dt
Multiply both sides by 2 to isolate d[B]/dt:
d[B]/dt = −(2/3)·d[A]/dt
The minus sign is there because A is being consumed, so d[A]/dt is itself negative — which makes
d[B]/dt positive, as it must be for a product.
Check the ratio: 2 moles of B appear for every 3 of A consumed, so B changes two-thirds as fast ✓
∴ d[B]/dt = −(2/3)·d[A]/dt.
kcet|Chemistry|2016|12||0|0:
Activation energy comes from the Arrhenius equation, k = Ae^(−Ea/RT).
Taking logarithms: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT
One measurement is not enough, because both A and Ea are unknown. Measure k at two
temperatures and subtract to eliminate A:
ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)·(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)
Everything else in that expression is known, so Ea follows directly.
(2) Changing concentration alters the rate but not the rate constant, so it tells you the order,
not Ea.
(3) Concentrations alone, without the rate constants, do not give Ea.
(4) A single k at one temperature leaves two unknowns and one equation.
∴ by evaluating rate constants at two different temperatures.
kcet|Chemistry|2016|13||0|0:
Find the false statement about physisorption.
(1) True — physisorption is held by van der Waals forces alone; that is its defining feature.
(2) True — a gas that liquefies easily has stronger intermolecular attraction and a higher critical
temperature, so it is adsorbed more readily.
(3) True — because the forces are non-specific, further layers can build on the first, so at high
pressure physisorption is multilayer. Chemisorption, needing a chemical bond to the surface,
stops at one layer.
(4) False — adsorption always *releases* energy. Molecules lose freedom of movement when they
stick to a surface, so ΔS is negative; for ΔG to be negative, ΔH must be negative too.
The magnitude is low, 20–40 kJ mol⁻¹, but the sign is negative, not positive.
∴ statement (4) is incorrect.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|14||0|0.s:
Colloids are classified by what the dispersed particle actually is.
Multimolecular colloids — a large number of small molecules or atoms cluster together until the
aggregate falls in the colloidal range, 1–1000 nm. They are held by weak van der Waals forces.
Macromolecular colloids — a single molecule is already big enough, as with starch or protein.
Associated colloids — small molecules that behave normally when dilute but form micelles above
a certain concentration, as with soap.
Sulphur sol belongs to the first class: it consists of thousands of S₈ molecules clustered into
aggregates of colloidal size. Not discrete atoms, and not single molecules.
A gold sol is the other standard example of the same type.
∴ large aggregates of S-molecules.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|15||0|0.s:
Zeolites are aluminosilicates with an open, honeycombed three-dimensional structure, and they
work as shape-selective catalysts.
The catalysis depends entirely on geometry. A reactant molecule can only react if it is small
enough to enter through the aperture, move along the pores and fit inside the cavity where the
active sites are. Anything larger is simply excluded, and product molecules too large to get back
out never escape.
So the pore structure, the aperture size and the cavity size all control which reactions happen —
which is why the same zeolite can convert one isomer and ignore another of the same formula.
ZSM-5 exploits exactly this to turn alcohols into petrol.
∴ all of these.
